name: Sundara Kanda
title: Sundara Kanda: Hanuman’s Journey to Lanka and Meeting with Sita
description: A detailed guide to Valmiki’s Sundara Kanda: the ocean crossing, Sita in Ashoka grove, Rama’s ring, Hanuman’s mission and the return, with chapter references.
dek: Hanuman can cross the sea. The harder task is to enter an enemy city, find someone who has almost lost hope, and speak in a way she can trust.
summary: Sundara Kanda follows Hanuman’s journey to Lanka, his discovery of Sita, their exchange of messages and tokens, his confrontation with Ravana’s forces and his return to Rama. Its central achievement is the restoration of communication between Rama and Sita.
editionNote: This guide follows K. M. K. Murthy’s 68-sarga Sundara Kanda at ValmikiRamayan.net. It is a guide to Valmiki’s Sanskrit narrative, not the differently structured Sundar Kand of the Ramcharitmanas or a prescribed recitation manual.

sections.heading: One crossing, several kinds of obstacle
paragraphs: Hanuman begins the leap after the preparations at the end of Kishkindha Kanda. The crossing is not a single display of speed. Mainaka offers rest, Surasa tests his ability to pass her demand, and Simhika seizes his shadow. Each encounter calls for a different response.

Hanuman acknowledges hospitality without abandoning the mission. With Surasa he uses a change of size and ingenuity; against Simhika he uses decisive force. The episode presents strength as the ability to judge what an obstacle requires, rather than the habit of treating every obstacle alike.
The preparation belongs to the previous book. For the distinction between the reminder and the leap, read [Jambavan’s encouragement in Kishkindha Kanda](/ramayana/kishkindha-kanda#jambavan).

sections.heading: Entering Lanka without announcing the mission
paragraphs: Arriving at Lanka, Hanuman examines its defences and considers how to move through it unseen. He reduces his form and enters at night, overcoming the city’s guardian. The vast scale of the leap gives way to the patience of a search.

He passes through palaces and private chambers, observing the wealth and life of Ravana’s city. The descriptions include the Pushpaka vehicle and the sleeping royal household. Finding women in the palace does not mean he has found Sita; he must interpret what he sees without allowing an expectation to become a false conclusion.

The search brings anxiety. Hanuman considers the consequences of returning without news and resists despair. His eventual decision to examine the Ashoka grove comes after sustained uncertainty. The narrative gives him judgment and vulnerability alongside extraordinary capability.

sections.heading: Sita’s refusal is the centre of the grove scene
paragraphs: Hanuman recognizes a woman whose condition and surroundings fit the person he seeks. Sita is guarded, distressed and separated from Rama. The splendour of Lanka does not make her situation fortunate; the narrative repeatedly places its wealth beside her suffering.

Ravana approaches and tries persuasion, promises and threats. Sita refuses him and directs him toward the consequences of his conduct. The rakshasi guards intensify the pressure after he leaves. Her speech matters because captivity has restricted her actions without obtaining her consent.

Trijata recounts a dream that points toward Rama’s victory and Ravana’s fall. Signs of hope appear amid Sita’s fear that time is running out. Hanuman watches before speaking, because an ill-judged approach could frighten the very person he has come to reassure.

sections.heading: Why Hanuman begins with a story
paragraphs: Hanuman considers how his language and appearance might be received. A sudden speech from an unfamiliar creature could seem like another deception by Ravana. He begins by recounting Rama’s story from concealment, giving Sita something recognizable before asking her to trust him.

The conversation develops through questions. Sita tests who he is and what he knows. Hanuman describes Rama and Lakshmana and explains the alliance with Sugriva. Rama’s ring then provides a material sign connected with the person whose story he has been telling.

The ring is not a magical substitute for communication. Its force comes from the surrounding exchange: a messenger, a remembered relationship and details that connect a claim with evidence. Sita moves from suspicion toward a guarded renewal of hope.

sections.heading: Why Sita does not leave on Hanuman’s back
paragraphs: Hanuman offers to carry Sita away. She raises several objections, including the dangers of the flight and a possible pursuit, the physical circumstances of being carried, and the importance of Rama confronting the captor himself. The passage should not be flattened into a claim that she rejects rescue for one simple reason.

Sita gives a personal token and messages for Rama. The remembered crow episode serves as another private sign. She also asks how an army could cross the sea, a practical question that Hanuman must answer without pretending that his own leap has solved every part of the war.

Hanuman reassures her about the strength of Rama’s allies. The conversation closes with a task still unfinished: her words and token must reach Rama. Finding her is only part of the messenger’s obligation.

sections.heading: Hanuman turns discovery into a confrontation
paragraphs: Before leaving, Hanuman decides to test the enemy’s strength and create an opportunity to address Ravana. He damages the grove, draws successive forces into battle and kills several opponents, including Aksha. The encounter with Indrajit eventually brings him before the king.

In Ravana’s court, Hanuman identifies himself as a messenger and warns of the consequences of keeping Sita. He does not present the coming war as inevitable regardless of Ravana’s choices: returning her remains the action that could avert catastrophe.

Ravana orders his death, but Vibhishana objects to killing a messenger. The objection establishes a limit even within a hostile court. Punishment is redirected toward Hanuman’s tail, setting up the next reversal.

sections.heading: Lanka burns, and Hanuman questions his own anger
paragraphs: Hanuman is paraded with his tail set alight. He escapes his restraints and uses the fire against the city. What was meant to humiliate a messenger becomes a public demonstration of Lanka’s vulnerability.

Then doubt interrupts triumph. Has Sita been harmed by the fire? Hanuman criticizes the danger of uncontrolled anger and seeks assurance of her safety. He returns to see her before leaving. The episode is richer when the self-questioning is read alongside the destruction.
The burning of Lanka does not complete Sita’s rescue or end Ravana’s rule. It changes the strategic and emotional circumstances, but the return of the messenger is still necessary.

sections.heading: The mission ends when Rama receives Sita’s words
paragraphs: Hanuman crosses back and rejoins the search party. Jambavan asks for a clear account. The companions discuss what should happen next, and the requirement to report to Rama keeps celebration from replacing the mission.

At Madhuvana the vanaras’ exuberance causes damage and provokes a complaint. Sugriva reads their behaviour as a sign of success. The search has returned from the edge of despair with news that changes everything.

Hanuman presents Sita’s token and repeats her messages. Rama asks to hear her words again. The close of the book turns from an extraordinary leap to the intimate need of one person to hear what another has said. [Yuddha Kanda](/ramayana/yuddha-kanda) begins with Rama’s response and the problem of bringing an army across the ocean.

sections.heading: Reading Sundara Kanda as story and devotion
paragraphs: Sundara Kanda has a major life in devotional recitation. This page explains the narrative and its questions; it does not prescribe one universal schedule or promise a particular material result from reading it. Practices differ between families, teachers and traditions.

The Sanskrit word sundara means beautiful, but explanations of the book’s title vary. Hanuman’s devotion, Sita’s endurance, the beauty of the poetry and the movement from despair toward hope all figure in later interpretation. A single explanation should not be presented as a settled statement by the narrator.

Readers arriving from a recitation of Tulsidas’s Sundar Kand should also note the change of text. The broad mission is familiar, but verse forms, chapter divisions and narrative details are not interchangeable.

questions.question: How many sargas are in Sundara Kanda?
questions.answer: The edition used here contains 68. A Sundar Kand in the Ramcharitmanas is a different text and should not be compared using this chapter count.

questions.question: Does Hanuman rescue Sita in Sundara Kanda?
questions.answer: He finds her, communicates with her and returns with her message. She remains in Lanka; the war and her release occur in Yuddha Kanda.

questions.question: What does Hanuman give Sita?
questions.answer: He gives her Rama’s ring as a sign of his mission. Sita gives him a personal ornament and messages to carry back to Rama.
